tool.name: ClipDataToAnalysisArea
tool.summary: Clips any mix of RASTERS and FEATURE CLASSES to an analysis area polygon in one run. Drag layers in from the map or browse and multi-select datasets from disk. The output format follows the workspace: a FOLDER gets shapefiles and GeoTIFFs, a GEODATABASE gets native feature classes and rasters. Optionally projects every output to one coordinate system, suggesting geographic transformations automatically -- and accepting several, because different source datums may each need their own. Optionally adds every clipped dataset to the map, symbolized like its source layer when the input came from the map. A modernized port of the CorridorDesigner Clip Analysis Layers tool. Needs no Spatial Analyst.
tool.usage:
WHY THIS TOOL EXISTS. A corridor or habitat analysis wants every input -- land cover, elevation, roads, streams, ownership -- trimmed to the same analysis area, and usually gathered into one workspace in one coordinate system. Doing that a dataset at a time means alternating between Clip (features), raster clipping, and Project, keeping formats and transformations straight by hand. This tool does the whole batch in one run: rasters and feature classes together, one analysis boundary, one destination, one optional coordinate system.
WHAT EACH DATASET GETS. Features are clipped with the standard Clip tool; rasters are clipped to the analysis area boundary (as a true clipping geometry, not just its rectangular extent) with no Spatial Analyst required. If an output coordinate system is set, each clipped result is then projected. Map layer selections are honored throughout: only the selected features of an input layer are clipped, and a selection on the analysis area layer limits the boundary. Each dataset is processed independently: one failure produces a warning and the batch continues, exactly like the original tool.
HOW RASTERS ARE PROJECTED. Rasters are ALWAYS projected with the NEAREST NEIGHBOR resampling technique: every output cell takes the value of the single nearest input cell, which never invents values that were not in the data -- required for categorical rasters (land cover, patch classes) and faithful, if slightly blockier, for continuous surfaces (elevation, distances). The OUTPUT CELL SIZE defaults to the input raster's own cell size expressed in the output coordinate system's units at the data's location, and the output grid's REGISTRATION POINT defaults to the lower-left corner of the projected extent. Because this tool honors the standard geoprocessing environments, you can control both explicitly: set the Cell Size environment to dictate the output resolution, or the Snap Raster environment to align the output cells with an existing raster's grid. If you prefer a different resampling technique for a particular raster (bilinear or cubic for a smooth surface, say), project that raster into the target coordinate system FIRST with Esri's Project Raster tool -- where you control the technique, cell size, and registration directly -- and then hand the projected copy to this tool; a raster already in the output coordinate system is clipped with no resampling at all.
GEOGRAPHIC TRANSFORMATIONS, SEVERAL AT ONCE. When the output coordinate system's datum differs from a source dataset's, a geographic transformation is needed -- and a mixed collection may need DIFFERENT ones (WGS 1984 sources and NAD 1927 sources both headed to NAD 1983, say). As soon as you pick the output coordinate system, the dialog fills the transformation list with a suggestion for every source datum present (the same extent-aware ranking the Project tool uses), and the dropdown offers all valid alternatives if you prefer a different path. At run time each dataset uses the first chosen transformation valid for its own datum pair; if none fits, the tool falls back to Esri's best suggestion and says so in the messages. Same-datum data needs no transformation and is not affected by any of this.
OUTPUT NAMES AND FORMATS. Outputs keep their source names, with the optional PREFIX and SUFFIX wrapped around them (a suffix like _clip keeps clipped outputs from ever shadowing same-named originals in the destination); if necessary, each name is automatically adjusted to meet the destination workspace's naming rules. A folder workspace writes shapefiles and GeoTIFFs; a geodatabase workspace writes native feature classes and rasters -- geodatabases are the recommended home. EXISTING DATA IS NEVER DELETED UNTIL ITS REPLACEMENT EXISTS: when an output name is already taken, the new dataset is produced under a temporary name first, and only a successful result replaces the old dataset (with overwrite-outputs enabled) or is kept under a numbered name (with it disabled) -- a failed clip can never cost you the dataset that was already there. With "Add clipped layer(s) to map" checked, every clipped dataset is added to the active map -- and an output whose input came in as a MAP LAYER is symbolized the same way that original layer was, so a clipped DEM looks like its source DEM (a dataset browsed from disk has no symbology to copy and gets Pro's default). Each output carries provenance metadata naming its source, the analysis area, and any projection applied.
ENVIRONMENTS. Unlike this toolbox's grid-native analysis tools, this is a data-preparation tool built on standard geoprocessing (Clip, Project, Project Raster), so the geoprocessing environment settings apply in the ordinary way.
CREDITS AND REFERENCES. The original CorridorDesigner Clip Analysis Layers tool is by Dan Majka (dan@corridordesign.org, 2006-2007); this ArcGIS Pro version is by Jeff Jenness and Dan Majka. Please cite: Majka, D., J. Jenness, and P. Beier. 2007. CorridorDesigner: ArcGIS tools for designing and evaluating corridors. http://corridordesign.org.

param.name: datasets
param.displayname: Datasets to clip (rasters and feature classes)

dialogReference.para: The rasters and feature classes to clip, in any mix. Drag layers in from the Contents pane, pick them from the dropdown, or click Browse and multi-select datasets from disk. Map layer selections are honored -- only the selected features are clipped.

The polygon boundary everything is clipped to. A map layer's active selection is honored, so you can clip to just the selected polygon(s). Rasters are clipped to the polygon shape itself, not merely its extent rectangle.

Where the clipped datasets go. A GEODATABASE (suggested by default) produces native feature classes and rasters -- the recommended choice. A FOLDER produces shapefiles and GeoTIFFs for workflows that need file-based data.
Text added to the START of every output name -- a project code, a species tag. If necessary, the name will be automatically adjusted to meet the workspace naming rules.

Text added to the END of every output name. Defaults to _clip, which guarantees the clipped outputs never collide with same-named source datasets living in the destination workspace; clear the box to keep the plain source names. If necessary, the name will be automatically adjusted to meet the workspace naming rules.

Project every clipped output to this coordinate system. Leave empty to keep each dataset's own coordinate system. Picking a system whose datum differs from a source dataset's fills the Geographic Transformations list automatically.

The datum transformations to use, one per source datum -- suggested automatically when you pick the output coordinate system (extent-aware, the same ranking the Project tool uses), with all valid alternatives in the dropdown. Several can be listed because different sources may need different datum paths; each dataset uses the first one valid for its own datum pair, falling back to Esri's suggestion with a message if none fits.

Checked (the default): every clipped dataset is added to the active map, and outputs whose inputs came in as MAP LAYERS are symbolized the same way those original layers were; datasets browsed from disk get Pro's default symbology. Unchecked: nothing is added to the map -- the outputs are simply written to the workspace.

scriptExample.title: Clip Data to Analysis Area example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Clips two rasters and two feature classes to a study area, gathering everything into one geodatabase in NAD 1983 UTM Zone 12N, with transformations for the WGS84 and NAD27 sources.
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
arcpy.jenness.ClipDataToAnalysisArea( [r"C:\data\landcover.tif", r"C:\data\dem.tif", r"C:\data\hydro.gdb\streams", r"C:\data\roads.shp"], r"C:\project\study_area.shp", r"C:\project\Analysis.gdb", "", "_clip", arcpy.SpatialReference(26912).exportToString(), ["WGS_1984_(ITRF00)_To_NAD_1983", "NAD_1927_To_NAD_1983_NADCON"])
